lesson.title: Source Transformation: Swapping Voltage and Current Sources
lesson.summary: Source transformation lets you convert a practical voltage source in series with a resistor into an equivalent practical current source in parallel with the same resistor, or vice versa, without changing how the rest of the circuit behaves.
lesson.body:
A real voltage source is never perfectly ideal, it always has some series resistance associated with it, and a real current source likewise always has some parallel resistance associated with it. It turns out that a practical voltage source, an ideal voltage source V_s in series with a resistor R, and a practical current source, an ideal current source I_s in parallel with that same resistor R, can be made electrically indistinguishable from the perspective of anything connected to their two terminals, as long as I_s equals V_s divided by R. This equivalence is called source transformation, and it is a direct application of the Thevenin equivalent idea you have already studied, essentially converting between the Thevenin form of a source and its Norton form.

The value of source transformation is purely practical: some circuits are much easier to simplify when a source looks like a current source feeding a parallel combination, because parallel resistors combine with simple reciprocal formulas, while other circuits are easier when a source looks like a voltage source feeding a series combination, because series resistors just add. Source transformation lets you flip a source back and forth between these two forms whenever it makes the surrounding algebra simpler, without changing the actual voltage or current delivered to whatever load is attached to the terminals.

Consider a practical voltage source made of a 12 volt ideal source in series with a 4 ohm resistor. Transforming it into a practical current source gives I_s equals V_s divided by R, that is 12 divided by 4, which is 3 amps, placed in parallel with that same 4 ohm resistor. Both of these are supposed to behave identically to any load connected across their terminals, so the transformation should be verifiable by attaching the same load to each version and confirming the answer matches.

Attach a 2 ohm load resistor to the original voltage source version: the load sees the 12 volt source through a series total resistance of 4 ohms plus 2 ohms, or 6 ohms, giving a current of 12 divided by 6, which is 2 amps, and a load voltage of 2 amps times 2 ohms, or 4 volts. Now attach the same 2 ohm load to the transformed current source version instead: the 3 amp source splits between the 4 ohm parallel resistor and the 2 ohm load using the current divider rule, giving the load current as 3 amps times 4 divided by the sum of 4 and 2, that is 3 times 4 divided by 6, which equals 2 amps, and the load voltage is again 2 amps times 2 ohms, or 4 volts. Both forms deliver identical current and voltage to the load, exactly as source transformation promises.

Because source transformation preserves everything a load can measure at the terminals, it is a completely safe and reversible tool for simplifying complicated circuits with multiple sources, letting you combine sources that would otherwise sit on opposite sides of a network into a single equivalent source before finishing the analysis.
